teaching.diagnosis: Ganglion Cyst of the Dorsal Wrist
teaching.one_liner: A benign, fluid-filled cyst from a wrist joint or tendon sheath that commonly fluctuates in size and may ache with activity.
differentials: Occult fracture or other bony mass
red_flags: Rapid growth, a fixed hard mass, neurologic symptoms, or atypical pain warrants further assessment

must_ask.say: Does the lump change size, and does activity make it ache?
Does it limit wrist movement or cause numbness, tingling, or weakness?
Would you prefer observation, or is pain or appearance making you consider treatment?

history.answer: I have a smooth, round bump on the back of my right wrist that seems to get bigger and smaller over time.
I first noticed the bump about six months ago.
It is right on the back of my right wrist, right over the joint.
It grew slowly when it first appeared, but it hasn't grown rapidly or suddenly ballooned in size.
There is just this single bump, roughly the size of a small marble, about one and a half centimeters across.
It feels smooth and firm like a small rubber ball, and it moves slightly under the skin when I press on it.
It is mostly painless and does not hurt to touch, though it feels a bit achy after heavy workouts.
The skin over it looks completely normal, and there are no moles, discoloration, or dark spots.
No, it has never bled, scabbed, or broken open.
No, there has never been any redness, warmth, pus, or bad odor.
There is no central hole or pore, and nothing cheesy or white has ever squeezed out.
Yes, it definitely swells up and aches a little after intense gymnastics practice or heavy lifting, then shrinks when I rest my wrist.
My wrist moves well, but it feels slightly tight when I bend my hand all the way backward.
No, I have not had any numbness, tingling, or weakness in my hand or fingers.
No, I have never had an injury, fracture, cut, or surgery on that wrist.
I have never tried to squeeze, pop, or drain it myself, and I haven't had any medical procedures done on it.
No fever, chills, night sweats, or unexplained weight loss.
I spend a normal amount of time outdoors, but I have never had a severe blistering sunburn.
No, neither I nor anyone in my family has ever had skin cancer, melanoma, or atypical moles.
No, I do not have diabetes, I have never had an organ transplant, and I am not taking any immunosuppressive medications.
I was wondering if it might be a joint fluid lump or some kind of bone cyst.
I am worried it might be a tumor or cancer, or that I might need major surgery on my wrist that could interfere with gymnastics.
I was hoping you could drain it or remove it so it stops bothering my wrist during training.
I would prefer having it aspirated or removed simply, and I would really like to avoid major wrist surgery if possible.
I have always been completely healthy with no chronic medical conditions.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or dietary supplements.
I have no known allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I do not smoke and have never smoked.
I only drink an occasional beer socially once or twice a month, nothing more.
I am a competitive gymnast and gymnastics coach, and I live on my own in an apartment.
My parents and siblings are all healthy, with no history of joint problems, cysts, or cancers.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, pulse 68 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, temperature 36.7 °C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Athletic young male sitting comfortably, appearing well-developed and in no acute distress.

A 1.5 cm smooth, firm, circumscribed round mass on the dorsal aspect of the right wrist over the scapholunate joint, which transilluminates brightly with a penlight and has no overlying erythema, warmth, punctum, or skin changes.
Full active and passive range of motion in bilateral wrists and fingers, with no joint warmth, swelling, or crepitus.
Normal 5/5 motor strength in wrist flexion, wrist extension, finger spread, and hand grip bilaterally.
Intact light touch sensation across the median, ulnar, and radial nerve distributions of both hands.
No palpable lymphadenopathy in the cervical or axillary regions.
